title: 26 U.S. Code Section 280C(c) Disallowance of Deduction
description: Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c), the research deduction is reduced by the credit unless a timely election takes a reduced credit of 79% of the gross credit.
summary: Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c), U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit under Section 41 must reduce their Section 174A research expense deduction by the full credit amount, unless they elect on a timely filed original return to take a reduced credit equal to 79% of the gross credit, preserving the full deduction.

body.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c), U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit under Section 41 must reduce their Section 174A research expense deduction by the full credit amount, unless they elect on a timely filed original return to take a reduced credit equal to 79% of the gross credit, preserving the full deduction.
Statutory Architecture and Legislative Rationale of IRC Section 280C(c)

Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 280C(c) establishes the mandatory federal coordination mechanism between the research and development (R&D) tax credit under IRC Section 41 and the deduction or capitalization of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under IRC Sections 174 and 174A. In the absence of a statutory limitation bridging these provisions, a commercial taxpayer incurring Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) would simultaneously claim a dollar-for-dollar deduction against taxable income under Section 174A (or amortization deductions under Section 174 or Section 174A(c)) and a direct dollar-for-dollar reduction in final tax liability under Section 41 for the identical capital outlay.

The legislative philosophy underlying Section 280C(c), as articulated by the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT), treats the Section 41 research credit as the economic equivalent of a direct federal grant, reimbursement, or subsidy for commercial research. Under foundational federal income tax policy, a taxpayer may not deduct ordinary and necessary trade or business expenses to the extent those outlays are effectively subsidized or reimbursed by the federal sovereign. Section 280C(c) enforces this prohibition against overlapping tax benefits through a bifurcated statutory structure that directly governs corporate effective tax rates, net operating loss (NOL) trajectories, cash flow profiles, and multi-state pass-through allocations.

Under the primary mandate of IRC Section 280C(c)(1), as amended by Section 70302(b)(2)(B) of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21), a taxpayer claiming the full, gross Section 41(a) research credit must reduce its domestic research or experimental expenditures (as defined in Section 174A(b)) otherwise taken into account as an immediate deduction under Section 174A(a) or charged to a capital account under Section 174A(c) by 100% of the research credit allowed under Section 41(a) for the taxable year. Recognizing that a mandatory deduction disallowance generates severe compliance and financial reporting friction—most notably by inflating federal taxable income through book-to-tax adjustments and transmitting artificial "phantom income" to pass-through owners—Congress enacted an elective escape valve in IRC Section 280C(c)(2), which was historically codified as Section 280C(c)(3) prior to the statutory redesignations of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, P.L. 115-97, Section 13206(d)(2)). Under Section 280C(c)(2)(A) and (B), a taxpayer may make an irrevocable annual election on a timely filed original return (including extensions) to reduce its Section 41(a) credit by the product of the gross credit and the maximum corporate tax rate in effect under IRC Section 11(b) (currently 21%), thereby preserving the full R&E deduction or capital account and bypassing the income add-back entirely. Furthermore, under IRC Section 280C(c)(3) (redesignated from former paragraph (4) by the TCJA), the controlled group rules of Section 280C(b)(3) apply for purposes of Section 280C(c).
Qualifying Expenditures and the IRC Section 41(d) Four-Part Test

The deduction disallowance rules of Section 280C(c) apply exclusively to the highly scrutinized subset of R&E expenditures that satisfy the statutory definition of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC Section 41(b) or basic research expenses under IRC Section 41(e)(2). General trade or business outlays deductible under IRC Section 162, or broader domestic and foreign R&E costs that qualify under Section 174 or Section 174A without meeting the narrower criteria of Section 41, fall outside the purview of Section 280C(c) and require no disallowance adjustment.

To generate QREs subject to the Section 280C(c) disallowance framework, a research activity must satisfy each element of the conjunctive four-part test codified in IRC Section 41(d). First, under the Section 174 / Section 174A eligibility test (updated by OBBBA Section 70302 in IRC Section 41(d)(1) to reference expenditures treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A), the expenditures must qualify as eligible research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174 or domestic research and experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174A, meaning they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process. Second, under the technological in nature test, the research activity must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, which requires that the process of experimentation fundamentally rely on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the business component test, the taxpayer must intend to apply the discovered information to develop a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, defined statutorily as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention that is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. Fourth, under the process of experimentation test, substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, which requires evaluating one or more alternatives through modeling, simulation, systematic trial and error, or similar methods to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain at the outset.

Specific statutory categories of direct in-house and third-party outlays incurred in executing activities that satisfy this four-part test enter the QRE computation base under IRC Section 41(b) and trigger downstream Section 280C(c) adjustments. Under IRC Section 41(b)(2) and (3), these eligible categories consist of W-2 taxable wages (as defined in IRC Section 3401(a), or self-employed earned income under IRC Section 401(c)(2), excluding wages taken into account in determining the Section 51 work opportunity credit) paid to employees for "qualified services"—which comprise directly performing, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research—the cost of tangible supplies (defined in Section 41(b)(2)(C) as any tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation) consumed directly in the conduct of qualified research (alongside eligible amounts paid or incurred for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research under Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)), and 65% of contract research expenses paid or incurred to third parties on the taxpayer's behalf under Section 41(b)(3)(A) (increasing to 75% for payments to qualified tax-exempt research consortia under Section 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for eligible energy research payments to small businesses, universities, and federal laboratories under Section 41(b)(3)(D)).
Federal Operational Mechanics of IRC Section 280C(c)

The operational choice between the gross credit path under Section 280C(c)(1) and the reduced credit election under Section 280C(c)(2) alters book-to-tax reconciliations, corporate effective tax rate calculations, liquidity profiles, and multi-jurisdictional tax liabilities.
The Gross Credit Path and Book-to-Tax Add-Backs (§ 280C(c)(1))

When a taxpayer claims the full gross research credit under Section 41(a) without making a Section 280C(c)(2) election, Section 280C(c)(1) enforces the deduction disallowance by eliminating a portion of the taxpayer's otherwise deductible domestic R&E expenses (or reducing the amount charged to the Section 174A(c) capital account) equal to the exact dollar amount of the gross credit allowed. From a financial accounting and corporate tax preparation standpoint, the taxpayer deducts the full R&E outlay on its financial statements and executes a permanent upward adjustment to federal taxable income on Schedule M-1 (for corporate entities with total assets below $10 million) or Schedule M-3 (for corporate entities with total assets of $10 million or more).

In the case of pass-through entities—specifically partnerships, limited liability companies (LLCs) taxed as partnerships, and S corporations—the Section 280C(c)(1) disallowance reduces entity-level ordinary business deductions and flows directly through to the individual partners or shareholders via Schedule K-1 pursuant to IRC Sections 702 and 1366. Because this upward income adjustment inflates the owners' federal adjusted gross income (AGI) and distributable net taxable income without any corresponding cash distribution, it generates artificial "phantom income". When partners or shareholders reside or file returns in state jurisdictions that conform to federal AGI or federal ordinary business income as their starting tax base but do not provide a corresponding state-level R&D tax credit or subtraction modification to offset the inflated income, the gross credit path forces the individual owners to pay state income tax on the federal Schedule M-1 or M-3 add-back.
The Reduced Credit Election (§ 280C(c)(2))

To eliminate the Schedule M-1/M-3 deduction add-back and prevent the transmission of pass-through phantom income, IRC Section 280C(c)(2) permits the taxpayer to affirmatively elect a mathematically reduced research credit. Under Section 280C(c)(2)(A) and (B), the elective credit equals the gross credit determined under Section 41(a) reduced by the product of the gross credit and the maximum corporate tax rate established under IRC Section 11(b) for the taxable year. Because the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 permanently fixed the maximum corporate income tax rate under Section 11(b) at 21%, the reduced credit is calculated by multiplying the gross credit by 79%.

For a profitable domestic C corporation paying tax at the statutory 21% rate entirely within the federal tax system, the net economic outcome is identical under either path. Under Section 280C(c)(1), claiming a $100,000 gross credit triggers a $100,000 income add-back that increases federal tax before credits by $21,000 ($100,000 × 21%), yielding a net federal tax reduction of $79,000. Under Section 280C(c)(2), claiming the $79,000 reduced credit leaves the $100,000 deduction intact, likewise yielding a net federal tax reduction of $79,000.

However, this theoretical parity breaks down rapidly across specific taxpayer profiles. For pass-through entities owned by individuals in high federal tax brackets, failing to make the Section 280C(c)(2) election forces partners or S corporation shareholders paying the top 37% individual marginal tax rate to suffer a 37-cent federal tax cost on every dollar of disallowed deduction while the Section 280C(c)(2) election reduces the credit by only the 21% corporate rate, creating a substantial federal and state tax disadvantage when the election is omitted. Conversely, for C corporations entrenched in deep net operating loss (NOL) positions, claiming the gross credit under Section 280C(c)(1) merely shrinks their growing NOL carryforward—a non-cash event in the current year—while preserving 100% of the dollar-for-dollar credit carryforward (which carries back 1 year and forward 20 years under IRC Section 39) for future profitable years. Parity similarly diverges for entities subject to the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) or for pre-revenue Qualified Small Businesses (QSBs) electing to apply the research credit against employer Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) and Medicare payroll taxes under IRC Section 41(h). Because a loss-making QSB cannot immediately utilize an income tax deduction, electing the reduced credit under Section 280C(c)(2) voluntarily surrenders 21% of immediate, liquid payroll tax cash flow merely to preserve an unutilized NOL carryforward.
Procedural Strictness: Form 6765 and Original Return Mandates

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) enforces the procedural requirements governing the Section 280C(c)(2) election with unyielding strictness. Pursuant to IRC Section 280C(c)(2)(C) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.280C-4(a), the election must be made on a timely filed original federal income tax return (including valid extensions) for the taxable year to which the election applies. The taxpayer effectuates the election by checking "Yes" on the designated reduced credit election box at the top of Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities—Item A for tax years 2024 and after, or Box 17 or Box 34 for tax years prior to 2024) and computing the 79% reduced credit directly on the face of the form.

Once made for a specific taxable year, the election is statutorily irrevocable. The IRS Office of Chief Counsel and Large and Mid-Sized Business (LMSB, now Large Business and International [LB&I]) directives maintain that taxpayers cannot make valid initial Section 280C(c) elections on amended returns under normal circumstances. Furthermore, administrative guidance issued via IRS Chief Counsel Generic Legal Advice Memorandum AM 2008-002 (dated February 8, 2008) and LMSB Directives explicitly invalidates conditional or "protective" Section 280C elections. While AM 2008-002 clarified that a taxpayer is treated as having made a valid reduced credit election if it clearly indicates its unconditional intent to claim the reduced credit on Form 6765 attached to a timely filed original return (even if the form initially reports zero or a nominal credit amount), a taxpayer cannot attach a conditional statement to an original return attempting to reserve the right to make a Section 280C election during a future audit or on a subsequent amended return, because any contingency in the taxpayer's intent invalidates the election. Consequently, any taxpayer that omits a valid election on its original return and later files an amended return (such as Form 1120X filed with the Ogden Service Center pursuant to Notice 2008-39) to claim the R&D credit is statutorily locked into claiming the gross credit under Section 280C(c)(1) and enduring the full Schedule M-1/M-3 deduction disallowance. In the LMSB Directive on Amended Returns/Refund Claims Containing Invalid I.R.C. § 280C(c)(3) Elections and Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 4.30.2, the IRS has instructed examiners that if a taxpayer fails to amend a refund claim to remove an invalid late election, the claim must be disallowed, penalties under IRC Sections 6694 and 6701 may apply, and practitioners who persistently file or advise taxpayers to file invalid late elections on amended returns and refuse to correct them should be formally referred to the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) for sanctions.
Legislative Evolution: From the PATH Act and TCJA to the OBBBA of 2025

Originally enacted in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 to stimulate private-sector innovation and extended temporarily 16 times before being made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (P.L. 114-113), the federal R&D tax credit regime underwent extraordinary structural metamorphosis between 2017 and 2026. These shifts were driven by changing macroeconomic policies governing the recovery of domestic and foreign R&E expenditures under IRC Sections 174 and 174A and their mechanical link to Section 280C(c).

body.text: The TCJA Era: Mandatory Capitalization and the "Excess" Anomaly (2022–2024)

Prior to the effective date of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA) R&E amendments, taxpayers immediately deducted their R&E expenditures in the year incurred under IRC Section 174(a), and Section 280C(c)(1) reduced that immediate deduction by the full gross credit. As a budget-reconciliation revenue-raising measure, TCJA Section 13206 amended Section 174 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, mandating that all specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures—prominently including all software development costs—could no longer be immediately expensed. Instead, SRE outlays had to be charged to a capital account and amortized ratably over five years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research, utilizing a mandatory mid-year convention.

This shift to mandatory amortization created a major unintended statutory loophole in the mechanics of Section 280C(c). TCJA Section 13206(d)(2)(A) amended Section 280C(c)(1) to state that the amount chargeable to the capital account for SRE expenditures had to be reduced only by the amount by which the Section 41(a)(1) research credit exceeded the amount allowable as an amortization deduction for qualified research expenses or basic research expenses for that specific taxable year. Because domestic SRE expenditures were amortized over five years using a mid-year convention, the allowable amortization deduction in the first year equaled 10% of the total incurred expenses.

In almost all commercial scenarios, the generated Section 41 R&D credit—which typically yields 6% to 10% of total QREs under the federal Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) methodology—did not mathematically exceed the 10% first-year amortized deduction. Because the research credit did not exceed the allowable current-year deduction, taxpayers were not statutorily required to reduce their capitalized SRE accounts at all. This drafting anomaly allowed corporations during the 2022–2024 period to claim the full, gross Section 41 credit without any corresponding reduction in their Section 174 capital account, resulting in a permanent 21% economic windfall compared to pre-TCJA law.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025

Responding to this statutory anomaly and sustained industry advocacy from the domestic technology, pharmaceutical, and manufacturing sectors, Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21, 139 Stat. 72), which was signed into law on July 4, 2025. Section 70302 of OBBBA restructured the federal R&E framework by enacting IRC Section 174A, which permanently reinstates immediate 100% expensing under Section 174A(a) for domestic research or experimental expenditures (including software development costs under Section 174A(d)(3)) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while also offering an election under Section 174A(c) to capitalize and amortize domestic R&E expenditures over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which benefits are first realized. At the same time, OBBBA Section 70302(b)(1) deliberately retained the 15-year capitalization and amortization requirement for foreign R&E expenditures under the amended Section 174 framework, establishing a stark geographic divergence designed to incentivize the onshoring of intellectual property development and scientific labor. Furthermore, OBBBA Section 70302(b)(1)(C) amended Section 174(d) to prohibit the immediate recovery of unamortized foreign R&E basis upon the disposition, retirement, or abandonment of property after May 12, 2025, trapping unamortized foreign expenditures on the balance sheet over the full 15-year recovery schedule.

Crucially, OBBBA Section 70302(b)(2)(B) completely rewrote IRC Section 280C(c)(1) to close the TCJA "excess" loophole. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, the revised statute provides that the domestic research or experimental expenditures (as defined in Section 174A(b)) otherwise taken into account as a deduction or charged to capital account under Chapter 1 shall be reduced by the full amount of the gross R&D credit allowed under Section 41(a), restoring the pre-TCJA mathematical trade-off. Consequently, electing the 79% reduced credit under Section 280C(c)(2) on a timely filed original return has returned as the primary mechanism for taxpayers seeking to avoid the full deduction disallowance.
Revenue Procedure 2025-28 and the Retroactive Amended Return Window

To facilitate the transition from the TCJA's capitalization regime to OBBBA's Section 174A expensing regime, the IRS released Revenue Procedure 2025-28 on August 28, 2025 (published in Internal Revenue Bulletin 2025-38 on September 15, 2025). Modifying Revenue Procedure 2025-23, this procedural guidance established automatic accounting method change rules under IRC Sections 446(e) and 481, permitting taxpayers under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2) to either immediately deduct all remaining unamortized domestic R&E costs from the 2022–2024 TCJA period in their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (the 2025 taxable year) or spread the accelerated recovery ratably over the two-taxable-year period comprising 2025 and 2026.

For Section 280C(c) tax planning, OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1)(D) and Sections 4 and 5 of Revenue Procedure 2025-28 provided a historic, one-time exception to the strict original-return-only mandate governing the reduced credit election. Eligible small businesses—defined as non-tax-shelter taxpayers satisfying the IRC Section 448(c) gross receipts test for their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, which required average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 2022–2024 period—that elected under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1)(A) and Section 3 of Revenue Procedure 2025-28 to apply Section 174A immediate expensing (and OBBBA-amended Section 280C(c)) retroactively to the 2022–2024 tax years were granted a temporary window to make a late Section 280C(c)(2) election, or revoke a prior Section 280C(c)(2) election, on amended returns or Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs). (Section 8 of Revenue Procedure 2025-28 also provided an automatic six-month extension to file superseding 2024 returns for eligible taxpayers that had filed original 2024 returns without an extension prior to September 15, 2025.) However, this statutory relief window was strictly temporary and permanently closed on July 6, 2026 (adjusted from July 3, 2026 because of the Independence Day legal holiday), or upon the expiration of the specific tax year's statute of limitations for refund claims under IRC Section 6511, whichever occurred first. Because the July 6, 2026 deadline has now passed, this retroactive relief window is definitively closed, and the strict prohibition against making or revoking Section 280C(c)(2) elections on amended returns has been fully reinstated by the IRS.
Federal Judicial Precedents Governing the QRE Base and Downstream Disallowance

Because the Section 280C(c) deduction disallowance is a direct mathematical function of the allowable Section 41 credit, federal court decisions restricting the qualification or substantiation of QREs directly alter the magnitude of a taxpayer's downstream Section 280C(c) adjustment. Both the U.S. Tax Court and the federal appellate circuits view the research credit as a matter of legislative grace requiring stringent substantiation.

In the foundational decision Eustace v. Commissioner, 312 F.3d 1254 (7th Cir. 2002), affirming T.C. Memo. 2001-66, the Seventh Circuit closely scrutinized retroactive R&D tax credit claims filed on amended returns on behalf of Applied Systems, Inc. (a Subchapter S corporation developing commercial software for insurance agencies) that relied on prepackaged accounting studies. The court reinforced the heavy burden of proof placed on taxpayers attempting to reclassify expenses as QREs retroactively without contemporaneous, project-level documentation linking employee activities to the four-part test, establishing a rigorous evidentiary bar for substantiating the base expenditures subject to Section 280C(c).

Similarly, in Estech Systems Inc. (Suder) v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, the U.S. Tax Court addressed the reasonableness standard of compensation under IRC Section 174(e). The court held that where compensation paid to corporate executives—specifically Eric Suder, the founder, chief executive officer, and 90% shareholder of S corporation Estech Systems, Inc.—is objectively unreasonable based on market standards, the excess compensation cannot qualify as a valid Section 174 expenditure. Because an expenditure must first satisfy Section 174 (and Section 174A) to qualify as a Section 41 wage QRE, striking down unreasonable executive compensation directly shrinks the eligible QRE pool and alters the entire downstream Section 280C(c) deduction disallowance calculation.

In Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), affirming the U.S. Tax Court (T.C. Memo. 2022-127; see also prior discovery proceedings at T.C. Memo. 2020-121), the Eighth Circuit clarified the boundaries of the "funded research" exclusion under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d), which disqualify research to the extent it is funded by any grant, contract, or another person. The Eighth Circuit ruled that commercial structural engineering contracts containing standard inspection, milestone acceptance, termination for substantial underperformance, and quality assurance provisions do not make payment contingent on the success of unproven research or place the ultimate economic risk of technological failure on the contractor, distinguishing between normal contractual performance barometers and contingent technological risk. Disqualifying contract outlays as funded research directly reduces the allowable credit and reshapes the deduction reduction modeling required under Section 280C(c). Furthermore, in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), affirming T.C. Memo. 2009-50, the Second Circuit restricted the eligibility of raw materials and routine supplies consumed during full-scale commercial production runs on which process research was conducted—holding that supplies the taxpayer would have purchased and used to produce goods for sale regardless of any research are ordinary production costs excluded from QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(1)—refining the boundaries of the supplies exclusion and base-period computations that govern the QRE pool subject to Section 280C(c).
State Conformity and Divergence: The California R&TC Section 24440 Framework

The systemic complexity of IRC Section 280C(c) intensifies when federal tax postures interact with state-level corporate and personal income tax regimes. While "rolling conformity" states automatically align their tax codes with federal IRC amendments as enacted, "static conformity" (or selective "specified-date conformity") states anchor their tax statutes to the Internal Revenue Code as it existed on a specific historical date while selectively decoupling from targeted federal provisions. This divergence frequently decouples state R&E deduction rules from federal mandates, requiring corporate tax departments to maintain separate financial models for federal and state Section 280C(c) compliance across jurisdictions such as California, New York, Texas, and Florida.
Statutory Structure of the California Research Credit (R&TC §§ 17052.12 and 23609)

California represents the most complex and consequential case study in state-level divergence. Administered by the California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) via Form FTB 3523 (Research Credit), the California R&D tax credit is codified under California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) Section 17052.12 for personal income tax purposes (including partnerships, LLCs taxed as partnerships, and individuals) and R&TC Section 23609 for corporate franchise and income tax purposes.

While California incorporates the foundational four-part test of IRC Section 41, it imposes an overarching geographic restriction: all qualified research and basic research activities must be conducted exclusively within the physical borders of California. This strict geographic mandate requires multi-state taxpayers to segregate California-based wages, supplies, computer rental costs, and contract research from out-of-state operations. Additionally, pursuant to R&TC Sections 17039.4 and 23036.4, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, California enacted a strict $5,000,000 annual limitation on the application of business tax credits—including current-year R&D credits and prior-year R&D credit carryovers (applied at the combined reporting group level)—to reduce net tax liability. Unused California research credits carry forward indefinitely, or taxpayers (other than S corporations with respect to entity-level credits) may make an irrevocable election on Form FTB 3870 with a timely filed original return to convert credits disallowed by the $5,000,000 cap into a refundable credit claimed at 20% annually over a five-year refundable period beginning the third taxable year after the election is made.

Furthermore, on October 1, 2025, California enacted Senate Bill 711 (SB 711, Chapter 231, Statutes of 2025), which updated California's general IRC conformity date from January 1, 2015, to January 1, 2025, and formally repealed California's three-tiered Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC, which had previously applied tiered rates of 1.49%, 1.98%, and 2.48%) effective for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025. In place of the repealed AIC, SB 711 amended R&TC Sections 17052.12(g)(2) and 23609(h)(2) (repealing the pre-2025 nonconformity rule of former R&TC Section 23609(h)(4)) to adopt a modified California Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) modeled on IRC Section 41(c)(4). Under SB 711 and the 2025 Form FTB 3523 instructions, taxpayers for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, must affirmatively elect on a timely filed original return between the Regular Credit (Section A of Form FTB 3523, equal to 15% of California QREs exceeding the California base amount, plus 24% of excess basic research payments for eligible corporations) and the new California Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) (Section B of Form FTB 3523, equal to a reduced rate of 3% of current-year California QREs exceeding 50% of the average California QREs for the three preceding taxable years, or 1.3% of current-year California QREs if the taxpayer had no California QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years, plus 24% of excess basic research payments for eligible corporations). A previous AIC election does not default to either method, and once a California ASC election is made on a timely filed original return, it applies to all subsequent taxable years unless revoked with formal FTB consent obtained prior to filing the original return via federal Form 3115 or Form 1128.
Decoupling from Federal Section 174 while Conforming to Section 280C(c)

Although SB 711 advanced California's general specified conformity date from January 1, 2015, to January 1, 2025, California explicitly decoupled from the federal TCJA mandate to capitalize and amortize R&E expenditures during the 2022–2024 period, explicitly continued that nonconformity to federal Section 174 amortization in SB 711 (under R&TC Sections 17270(c), 24365, and 24440), and likewise does not conform to OBBBA's 15-year foreign R&E capitalization rule enacted in July 2025. Throughout the TCJA era and continuing into the present, California has continuously allowed taxpayers to immediately expense 100% of both their domestic and foreign R&E costs for state tax purposes.

However, under R&TC Section 24440 for corporations (and R&TC Section 17270 for personal income tax), California explicitly conforms to the deduction disallowance principles of IRC Section 280C(c). When a taxpayer claims the gross California R&D credit on Form FTB 3523 (Line 17a for the Regular Credit or Line 31a for the ASC), R&TC Section 24440 requires the taxpayer to reduce its state-level R&E deduction by the full amount of the California credit generated and attach a schedule listing the reduced deduction amounts. To avoid this state add-back, California permits taxpayers to make a state-level Reduced Credit Election (RCE) on Form FTB 3523 (Line 17b for the Regular Credit or Line 31b for the ASC). Crucially, the FTB recognizes that a taxpayer's federal and state tax postures are distinct and therefore permits taxpayers to make an independent Section 280C(c) election for California purposes on a timely filed original state return, completely decoupled from their federal choice on Form 6765. Because California preserves immediate R&E expensing (which offsets C-corporation income taxed at 8.84%) while capping credit utilization at $5,000,000 per year through 2026 and generating non-refundable credit carryforwards, electing the state reduced credit preserves immediate state deduction value and cash flow.
California Entity-Specific Reduced Credit Multipliers and Pass-Through Rules

Unlike the federal reduced credit election—which applies a flat 21% reduction (79% multiplier) to all taxpayers based on the top corporate tax rate under IRC Section 11(b)—California R&TC Section 24440(b)(3) (together with R&TC Sections 17052.12 and 23609 and Form FTB 3523) mandates that the state reduced credit multiplier vary according to the specific legal entity classification of the taxpayer or partner receiving the credit allocation. Specifically, C corporations multiply their gross California credit by 91.16% (reflecting 100% − 8.84% standard corporate franchise tax rate under R&TC Section 23151), individuals, estates, and trusts multiply their gross credit by 87.70% (reflecting 100% − 12.30% top base individual marginal rate), and S corporations compute their entity-level credit using a 98.50% multiplier (reflecting 100% − 1.50% S-corporation entity-level tax rate under R&TC Section 23802).

body.text: For pass-through structures, these tiered multipliers require careful partner-level tracking. Because tax credits are non-deductible tax items that do not adjust a partner's capital account, partnership allocations of the California research credit must satisfy the Partners' Interests in the Partnership (PIP) test under FTB rules, ensuring the credit is strictly allocated to the partners who bore the economic cost of the underlying QREs and preventing manipulative "credit stripping". For an S corporation, the entity itself may claim only one-third (33.3%) of the computed reduced credit (after applying the 98.50% multiplier) against its 1.50% entity-level franchise tax under R&TC Section 23803(a)(1) (subject to the $800 minimum franchise tax), while the remaining two-thirds of the entity-level credit is permanently disregarded and may not be used as a carryover under R&TC Section 23803(a)(2)(B). Simultaneously, under R&TC Section 23803(a)(2)(F), 100% of the full research credit computed under the Personal Income Tax Law passes through on a pro-rata basis to the S-corporation shareholders on Schedule K-1 (100S), who must then apply the 87.70% individual reduction rate on their personal California tax returns when the reduced credit election has been made (subject to the pass-through limitation of IRC Section 41(g)).
FTB Administrative Rulings on Gross Receipts, Throwback Sales, and Start-Ups

Executive branch guidance from the California FTB directly shapes the calculation of the regular incremental credit base and the resulting R&TC Section 24440 disallowance. A critical component of the California regular credit computation on Section A of Form FTB 3523 (Line 11) is the taxpayer's California gross receipts denominator for the four preceding taxable years, which dictates the base amount (Line 12) that current-year QREs must exceed. In FTB Technical Advice Memorandum (TAM) 2022-01 (and revised FTB Publication 1050), the agency adopted the Multistate Tax Commission's (MTC) August 2021 narrow interpretation of Public Law 86-272 (15 U.S.C. §§ 381–384) regarding internet sales and website activities. Under TAM 2022-01 and Publication 1050, if a company engages in non-protected interactive internet activities—such as offering online applications for non-sales job positions, placing internet cookies on customer computers to gather market research, or providing interactive post-sale assistance via electronic chat or email on a website—in a destination state where it lacks physical presence, the FTB deems the company to have exceeded P.L. 86-272 immunity and established income tax nexus in that destination state.

This nexus determination directly alters California's "throwback sales" rule under R&TC Section 25135. When a California-based R&D company ships tangible personal property to a customer in a destination state such as Nevada where it has no physical footprint, but its website activities establish destination nexus under TAM 2022-01, those sales are no longer thrown back into the California sales numerator. Excluding those throwback sales reduces the California gross receipts denominator on Line 11 of Form FTB 3523, lowers the base amount on Line 12 for the California R&D credit, increases the total state credit generated, and expands the subsequent R&TC Section 24440 deduction disallowance. This administrative interpretation has been the subject of major litigation in American Catalog Mailers Association (ACMA) v. Franchise Tax Board, Case No. CGC-22-601363, in the San Francisco County Superior Court of California, where on December 13, 2023, the court granted summary judgment in favor of ACMA and ruled both TAM 2022-01 and Publication 1050 invalid as "underground regulations" enacted without complying with the California Administrative Procedure Act (Cal. Gov't Code § 11340 et seq.). Additionally, for start-up companies that have "zero gross receipts" for California purposes during historical base years, FTB Legal Division Guidance 2012-03-01 confirms that such entities are not barred from claiming the California research credit under R&TC Section 23609; instead, they may utilize the regular incremental credit methodology under the statutory start-up rules (or, beginning in 2025, elect the new 3% / 1.3% California ASC under SB 711), allowing pre-revenue technology firms to generate credit carryforwards subject to Section 280C(c) and R&TC Section 24440 modeling.
Comprehensive Hypothetical Modeling: Post-OBBBA Section 280C(c) Elections

To illustrate the operational impact of Section 280C(c) and R&TC Section 24440 decisions under the post-OBBBA regime, consider a hypothetical financial model for a domestic enterprise operating exclusively in California during the 2025 taxable year. In this hypothetical scenario, the taxpayer generates $10,000,000 in pre-R&E taxable income for both federal and California purposes and incurs $1,000,000 in eligible domestic California-situs QREs, which are 100% immediately deductible federally under IRC Section 174A(a) and in California under state law. Based on these outlays, the taxpayer generates a federal gross R&D credit of $100,000 under IRC Section 41(a) and a California gross R&D credit of $100,000 under R&TC Section 23609.
Scenario A vs. Scenario B: C-Corporation Step-by-Step Reconciliation

When the taxpayer is structured as a standard C corporation, evaluating the gross credit path with a deduction disallowance (Scenario A) against the reduced credit election with full deduction preservation (Scenario B) demonstrates complete bottom-line net tax parity alongside a $100,000 divergence in adjusted taxable income.

headers: California Scenario B: Reduced Credit (R&TC § 24440 / Form 3523)

body.text: In this isolated C-corporation model, under Scenario A, the taxpayer deducts $1,000,000 under IRC Section 174A and adds back $100,000 on Schedule M-1 under Section 280C(c)(1), resulting in $9,100,000 of federal taxable income, $1,911,000 of gross federal tax at 21%, and $1,811,000 of net federal tax after applying the $100,000 gross credit. In California under Scenario A, the $100,000 R&TC Section 24440 add-back similarly yields $9,100,000 of state taxable income, $804,440 of gross tax at 8.84%, and $704,440 of net state tax after applying the $100,000 state credit. Under Scenario B, electing the reduced credit eliminates the $100,000 add-back in both jurisdictions, keeping taxable income at $9,000,000 and producing $1,890,000 of gross federal tax offset by a $79,000 reduced credit ($1,811,000 net federal tax) and $795,600 of gross California tax offset by a $91,160 reduced credit ($704,440 net state tax). If the taxpayer claimed the gross credit federally (Scenario A) but elected the reduced credit in California (Scenario B), a state subtraction adjustment would be required on the California return to eliminate the federal Section 280C(c)(1) income add-back before arriving at California taxable income.
Scenario C: The Multi-State Pass-Through Entity Vulnerability

When the identical hypothetical enterprise is structured as a multi-state pass-through entity—such as an LLC taxed as a partnership—rather than a C corporation, the economic outcome shifts dramatically against Scenario A. Under Scenario A, claiming the $100,000 gross federal credit requires a $100,000 federal Schedule M-1 income add-back at the partnership level, causing $100,000 of artificial phantom income to flow through to the individual partners on Schedule K-1.

Although the partners may claim their distributive share of the federal R&D credit on their individual federal returns, their federal adjusted gross income (AGI) is permanently inflated by $100,000. In addition to facing a top 37% federal individual marginal rate on that $100,000 add-back (which exceeds the 21% reduction rate under Section 280C(c)(2)), partners residing in states that impose an individual income tax tied to federal AGI without providing an offsetting state-level R&D credit or subtraction modification are forced to pay out-of-pocket state income tax on the $100,000 of phantom income. By executing Scenario B and making the federal Section 280C(c)(2) Reduced Credit Election, the partnership generates a $79,000 federal credit while maintaining clean Schedule K-1 taxable income at $9,000,000, completely shielding the partners from cross-border phantom income taxation.
The Intersection of IRC Section 280C(c) and the QSB Payroll Tax Credit (§ 41(h))

The strategic analysis of Section 280C(c) reverses completely when applied to early-stage technology and biotechnology startups that utilize the Qualified Small Business (QSB) payroll tax election under IRC Section 41(h). Enacted as part of the PATH Act of 2015, Section 41(h) permits startups with less than $5,000,000 in current-year gross receipts and zero gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the five-taxable-year period ending with the current year to elect to apply their generated R&D credit against the employer portion of their payroll tax liabilities.

When a QSB makes the Section 41(h) payroll tax election, the elected credit portion is recharacterized under Section 41(h)(2) so that it is no longer treated as an income tax credit for general purposes, except for the strict application of the Section 280C(c) deduction disallowance rules.

headers: Operational & Cash Flow Implications under IRC § 280C(c)

cells: Maximizes the immediate liquid cash benefit against quarterly employer payroll taxes ($100,000 cash offset on a $100,000 credit, up to the $500,000 annual ceiling). Requires a $100,000 add-back to taxable income under § 280C(c)(1), which merely reduces the loss-making startup's NOL carryforward (a non-cash event in the current year).

Reduces the available payroll tax offset by 21%. A $100,000 gross credit is reduced to $79,000, sacrificing $21,000 in immediate liquid cash simply to preserve an income tax deduction (NOL carryforward) that a pre-revenue startup may not utilize for years.

body.text: For a venture-funded QSB operating in a loss position with no immediate prospect of positive taxable income, electing the reduced credit under Section 280C(c)(2) constitutes a severe planning error. Checking the Section 280C(c)(2) box voluntarily surrenders 21% of the immediate liquid cash value of the payroll tax offset merely to preserve an income tax deduction that has a current cash value of zero.
Conclusion

IRC Section 280C(c) operates not as a mere ministerial checkbox on Form 6765, but as a foundational balancing mechanism of federal tax law designed to prevent the double subsidization of commercial research expenditures. The legislative trajectory from the TCJA's mandatory capitalization regime—which inadvertently rendered Section 280C(c)(1) an exploitable "excess" anomaly during 2022–2024—to the corrective enactment of IRC Section 174A and the restoration of the full deduction disallowance under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 underscores the financial significance of this provision.

For corporate and pass-through taxpayers alike, particularly those operating in selectively conforming states such as California under R&TC Section 24440 and SB 711 or allocating credits and income across multi-state partner bases, failing to model the downstream effects of the Section 280C(c) election can trigger uncompensated phantom income taxes or forfeit immediate payroll tax liquidity. With the permanent closure of the temporary Revenue Procedure 2025-28 amended return relief window on July 6, 2026, taxpayers and practitioners must execute rigorous, entity-specific forecasting prior to the filing of original returns to align federal and state Section 280C(c) elections with organizational liquidity and effective tax rate objectives.
